questions.prompt: Who has the puck?
questions.explanation: The setup names YOU as the puck owner. That makes carrying, protecting, or passing your next decision.

questions.prompt: Which two clues shape your carry?
questions.explanation: Gold1 blocks the straight route and Navy2 gives a wide navy option. Those locations matter more than simply moving forward.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in the upper open side before carrying.
questions.explanation: This moves YOU away from Gold1's straight path and toward the side where Navy2 waits. It is a useful example, not a required skating line.

questions.prompt: Arrange a safe carry check.
questions.explanation: Gold1 explains why the straight path is crowded. Move toward the visible room, then look again because that room can change.

questions.prompt: Gold1 shifts toward the upper side. What should you do?

options.text: Look for a new lane or use Navy2 if the pass is clear
Keep the same turn because it was open before
Drop the stick and stop watching

questions.explanation: Gold1 changes the upper-side condition. A new look may show another carry lane or a clear pass to Navy2; the answer depends on what remains open.

questions.prompt: Why keep your feet moving toward room?
questions.explanation: Moving toward visible room can give YOU time and space to handle the puck. Keep checking Gold1 and Navy2 because room is a changing condition.

scenarios.title: Show the middle for a pass
scenarios.objective: Move to a visible passing angle and recognize when a teammate is ready.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end and gold attacks the -x end. Navy2 has the puck near the boards. YOU wait below the puck carrier. Gold1 is between YOU and the middle. The coach asks you to move where Navy2 can see you, then check the lane.
cues: Gold1 sits between the first line and middle.

scenarios.limits: Static practice illustration. A visible facing direction is an authored cue, not proof that a player looked. An adult may read the questions aloud.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is the named puck owner. YOU are the possible receiver, so your job is to become useful to that carrier.

questions.prompt: What can help Navy2 find a pass?

options.text: Show your stick in open ice

questions.explanation: Moving to a different angle and showing a target can make YOU easier to see. Gold1 between the players means the first line needs a new look.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in open middle space where Navy2 can see you.
questions.explanation: This spot changes the angle around Gold1 and gives Navy2 a visible target. Another clear angle may work if the lane remains usable.

questions.prompt: Put the support read in order.

options.text: Show a target and check again

questions.explanation: Know who has the puck, move so Gold1 is not in the first lane, then show where a pass could go. The last check protects against a changing lane.

questions.prompt: Gold1 follows your first move. What is a useful change?

options.text: Move again to a clear angle
Stand still because Navy2 saw you once

questions.explanation: Gold1 taking away the first angle means YOU should help create another one. A different clear angle can keep a pass possible; it is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Why does your place matter to Navy2?
questions.explanation: Navy2 needs a target and a lane they can see. Moving around Gold1 can give the carrier a clearer choice while keeping YOU available.

scenarios.title: Help when the puck changes teams
scenarios.objective: Recognize a change from attacking to defending and choose a helpful route back.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end and gold attacks the -x end. Gold1 has just taken the puck near the middle. YOU are above the play and Navy2 is between YOU and the navy end. The coach says the team roles changed when Gold1 got the puck.
cues: Navy2 is closer to the navy end.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck now?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is the puck owner in this freeze. That means navy players need to think about helping defend.

questions.prompt: What should YOU notice after the change?

options.text: Navy2 is nearer the navy end
YOU should stay in the attacking end

questions.explanation: The new owner and the teammate nearer the navy end show the defensive picture. Staying high without checking leaves the puck carrier more room.

questions.prompt: Place YOU between Gold1 and the navy end to help.
questions.explanation: This example brings YOU back toward the play and the navy end while keeping Gold1 in view. The best route depends on the moving players.

questions.prompt: Arrange the role-change read.

options.text: Skate back while watching the play

questions.explanation: Recognize the new owner, turn toward the end you protect, and skate back while keeping the puck picture. The order teaches awareness before effort.

questions.prompt: Gold1 moves toward the lower side. What should guide YOU?

options.text: Keep the puck carrier and Navy2 in view
Chase only the nearest navy player
Stop watching because Navy2 is closer

questions.explanation: Gold1's new side changes the route. Seeing both the puck carrier and Navy2 helps YOU support the play without guessing where to skate.

questions.prompt: Why did your job change when Gold1 got the puck?
questions.explanation: Navy no longer controls the puck, so helping protect the navy end matters first. Turning back and watching Gold1 lets YOU choose a useful support route.

scenarios.limits: Static small-area illustration. The net is represented by the attacking end direction; no shot result, crease rule, or contact action is inferred. An adult may read the questions aloud.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck?
questions.explanation: Navy2 owns the puck. YOU are an off-puck teammate who can help by finding useful space.

questions.prompt: What makes this a crowded spot?

options.text: Navy2 is on the other team

questions.explanation: The navy players are close and Gold1 is in the goalward picture. Spreading to another angle may give the puck carrier more room.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in open space above Navy2, still near the play.
questions.explanation: This creates separation from Navy2 and a different passing angle while keeping YOU near the attacking play. A clear nearby spot can also work.

questions.prompt: Put this support move in order.

options.text: Move out of the crowded spot
Show a target and check Gold1

questions.explanation: Start with the puck carrier, create room, then show a target while checking the defender. Each step keeps the choice tied to the actual players.

questions.prompt: Gold1 leaves the net side and follows YOU. What is a good next read?

options.text: Find another clear place and keep Navy2 in view
Stay in the same place because it was open

questions.explanation: Gold1 changed the space YOU chose. Another angle may help Navy2, but it should be checked against the puck and the new defender position.

questions.prompt: Why make room for Navy2?
questions.explanation: Standing beside the puck carrier can crowd the play. A little separation gives Navy2 another visible target and more room to handle the puck, if Gold1 does not close it.

scenarios.title: Turn your body to the safe side
scenarios.objective: Use body position and a changing pressure cue to protect a loose carry.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end and gold attacks the -x end. YOU have the puck beside the boards. Gold1 is on your inside side. Navy2 is farther ahead on the wall side. The coach asks you to keep the puck away from Gold1 and look for Navy2.
cues: YOU have the puck by the boards.
Navy2 is ahead on the wall side.

scenarios.limits: Static practice freeze. It does not show contact, speed, handedness, or an escape with no pressure. An adult may read the questions aloud.

questions.prompt: Who is inside YOU?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is on the inside side of YOU. That pressure cue makes a direct inside move less comfortable.

questions.prompt: What can help protect the puck?

options.text: Keep your body between Gold1 and the puck

questions.explanation: Using your body as a shield and finding a teammate can protect the next touch. Pushing is not a safe puck-control choice.

questions.prompt: Place YOU a little closer to the wall side, away from Gold1.
questions.explanation: This example gives YOU more wall-side space from Gold1 and keeps Navy2 in the forward picture. Another controlled spot can work.

questions.prompt: Put the protection read in order.

options.text: Keep the puck on the far side
Look for Navy2 or new room

questions.explanation: The defender's side tells you where the first pressure is. Protect there, then scan for a teammate or a better lane.

questions.prompt: Gold1 reaches the wall side too. What is a smart update?

options.text: Look for another lane before carrying on
Keep the puck there without looking
Assume Navy2 can see through Gold1

questions.explanation: Gold1 has changed the wall-side option. A new look may show a turn, a pass to Navy2, or a safer hold; the picture decides.

questions.prompt: Why keep the puck away from Gold1?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is inside YOU, so the puck is easier to reach there. Keeping your body between the defender and puck can buy a moment to see Navy2 or another lane.
